newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian foreign reserves drop, riel "volatile".
newsitem.headline: Cambodian foreign reserves drop, riel "volatile".

text.p: Cambodia's foreign exchange reserves have dropped sharply and threaten to destabilise the national currency, financial analysts said on Thursday.

One economist said government statistics showed net foreign reserves had dropped as much as $20 million in the past few months to just above minimum levels set by the International Monetary Fund, raising concerns the Cambodian riel could be headed for a downward slide.
"The riel is very, very volatile," the economist said.

The IMF, which sets quarterly benchmark figures for foreign reserves in Cambodia -- a country whose economy has been shattered by more than two decades of war -- had set a minimum of $142.1 million for September.
The central bank's foreign reserves typically exceed benchmarks by $10 to $20 million, but September reports show the reserves at only $146.4 million.
The riel, which started the year at 2,550 to the dollar, slid to 2,945 in late August. It is currently trading at about 2,740, a central bank official said.

Citing a leaked confidential letter the central bank governor sent to co-premiers Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh, former deputy bank chief Tioulong Saumura told Reuters that in October, foreign reserves fell below levels recommended by the IMF.
"The central bank does not appear to have enough foreign reserves to protect the value of the riel," she said.
A copy of the letter written by National Bank of Cambodia Governor Thor Peng Leath, dated October 21 and seen by Reuters, said:
"The foreign reserves have decreased to a level below the benchmark set by the IMF and may decrease even further, leading to a crisis situation."
Thor Peng Leath could not be reached for comment, but a top central bank official dismissed the concerns and said the foreign reserves had since risen above benchmark levels.
The letter was written 10 days before an IMF delegation arrived in Phnom Penh to discuss lack of transparency in government accounting procedures.
The IMF has threatened to suspend the future disbursement of $60 million in loans unless the government fixed the problems.
It was expected to render a decision on the loans, which support the central bank, later on Thursday.

Tioulong Saumura, who resigned from her post in September 1995 over issues of reform at the bank, said she believed the foreign reserves woes were triggered by diversion of state revenues, government overspending and speculation on the riel.
The economist said the reserves remained "very close to IMF limits," and added that he was concerned about what action the central bank would take to address heavy government spending.
The IMF is in the second year of a three-year, $120-million loan package to Cambodia. Three $20 million installments have been issued to the government so far.
